title: UnitedHealth Group Deserves Our Congratulations, Today.
subtitle: I can absolutely believe UnitedHealth Group wins in court, often.
body_html:
UnitedHealth Group deserved some good news. They have had a really challenging year. It started with change healthcare, as amply covered in this newsletter. It continued with a department of justice investigation into insider trading… or at least, I strongly suspect, given the preservation of records request with which were hit with.

It continued with the murder of Brian Thompson, a horrifying act in the streets of New York City that, again, is not OK.

However, in the past week, we've gotten some really good news for UnitedHealth Group. They deserve congratulations. They beat a department of justice investigation, and as long as legal decisions are the standard of truth in America, which I hope they will continue to be for a variety of reasons for a good long time, today is the day I say good job UnitedHealth Group and I have to assume Justice was served.

I also wanna take a moment to explain why I'm writing an article congratulating United on something, anything. My readers might notice that I criticize united a lot.

For people who are new to reading this newsletter, here is an example of the many cases in which I'm making fun of or directly criticizing United's business practices:

  • I've criticized their compliance with fiduciary duty, under ERISA.

  • I have criticized their absurd denials of care.

  • I have criticized their compliance with privacy laws.

  • I've written satirical press releases, comparing them to the biblical leviathan.

  • I have written satirical press releases after the imagined acquisition of the middle earth kingdom of Mordor.

  • I have written satirical articles about their acquisition of great white shark nurseries off the coast of Long Island.

However, at the end of the day, UnitedHealth Group is on team healthcare. Either they're gonna be part of the solution, or they're gonna be part of the problem. I'm trying to convince them to be part of the solution. I do that through some degree of cajoling, but if it's just criticism, it's not really meeting my goals. I want healthcare to be better for patients. I had ideally like healthcare to also be better for doctors, because at the end of the day, I think that's better for patients. I would like patience and doctors to stand together, getting patients better, and making it more tolerable to do so. I think that can probably be aligned with a better business strategy for healthcare payors. But that means they have to join us in that mission. I spent a lot of time thinking about the people who work at United. There are people a lot like me. At one point in time I even applied to work there. I wrote a hit (and humorous) article about it. United doesn't advertise saying “help us ruin healthcare.” they may be ruining healthcare, practically, but they're not trying to run healthcare. They're trying to run a business. And the people who go work there are generally want to work in healthcare. These are my colleagues. These are my friends. These are people with similar goals in life to me, and too many of the people I know. I don't think the people who work at United healthcare are bad people. I think they're probably pretty good people who wanna make a change and see a huge organization has an opportunity to do that with a lot of support and resources. That's a relatable state of affairs for me. So I feel that my goal, has an author, is to convince United healthcare, and other companies like it, to make better decisions.

And, for me, the bottom line is that's more than just criticism. When criticism is due, it should be leveled. But I ceased to become a fair observer of the world when I don't congratulate them when they do things right. In fact, I think it's probably more important to highlight when they do things right than simply to harp on when they do things wrong. I have an opinion about what right is, and an opinion about what wrong is, and as a child psychiatrist, I'm pretty familiar with the fact that behavior is reinforced by attention. And when I pay attention to the good things that United does, and the people at United do, I'm hoping it will influence their behavior so they do more of it.

So today, here's what happened with the department of justice, here's how united beat the case, and here's what I'd like to see more of from United healthcare and United health group, it's parent organization.

There is the concept in the law of a qui tam lawsuit. It’s latin, for on behalf of the king.

​​These are litigation is brought by private citizens on behalf of the government. Usually, it's a case where the whistleblower brings a case for a crime where the government is a victim. So for example, a whistleblower might bring a lawsuit claiming Medicare or Medicaid fraud, or a kickback. One such case here in New York involved in a case against an Addiction Treatment Center (named ACI) with the Attorney General of the State of New York…for accepting kickbacks. Medicare and Medicaid are frequent sources of fraud and abuse. A devious character can just submit claims endlessly, and often get them paid. If what you're doing is criminal and not legal medical care? Well, you can make a lot of money while you're waiting for the government to figure it out and put a stop to your behavior.

In a qui tam case, a private citizen whistleblower, files a lawsuit on behalf of the government. They're incentivize to do this because if they win, they get to keep a percentage of the money the government would recoup. It's a way to incentivize individuals to blow the whistle on big companies that are defrauding the government.

Back in 2017, a whistleblower inside United Healthcare—now part of the larger UnitedHealth Group—had a lawsuit. They filed against United health group as a qui tam case. This was later taken over by the Department of Justice. Sometimes these cases that the government doesn't leave it to the whistleblower, they bring it inside the DOJ. In this case, the claim was as follows:

The United States has intervened and filed a complaint in a lawsuit against UnitedHealth Group Inc. (UHG) that alleges UHG obtained inflated risk adjustment payments based on untruthful and inaccurate information about the health status of beneficiaries enrolled in UHG’s largest Medicare Advantage Plan, UHC of California, the Justice Department announced today.

Later in the press release from DOJ, they clarify:

The lawsuit was filed by James Swoben, a former employee of Senior Care Action Network (SCAN) Health Plan and a consultant to the risk adjustment industry. The lawsuit was filed under the qui tam provisions of the False Claims Act, which permit private parties to sue on behalf of the United States for false claims for government funds, and to receive a share of any recovery. The False Claims Act permits the government to intervene in such a lawsuit, as it has done, in part, in this case.

It's really important to remember that when the government brings a lawsuit against you, either civilly or criminally, and they issue these very scary press releases, these are allegations the government is making.

The government, which can appeal, have not proved them to be true, at least as of this week. The government makes an allegation, and they putting out a press release. That press release serves a purpose— they can scare up additional witnesses, for example. They need to prove their case, but they haven't done it yet. And even when it comes to a behemoth like UnitedHealth Group, the United States Government is still bigger and slightly scarier. They can put you in jail. United healthcare can't do that. The government has to earn its convictions by actually proving a case in a court of law. In this particular case, in which it was alleged that United defrauded Medicare, they did not make their case in a court of law. Which means, and this is really important, they're not guilty.

Not beyond a reasonable doubt. I am a big fan of the rule of law here in America. If you can't make your case as the government, with all the tremendous resources of the Federal Government behind you, well, then you can just back the F- off. As citizens, we need to respect that the government has an unbelievable amount of fire power behind its ability to bring a prosecution. If they can't make a case, then there's not a case to be made. The tremendous power of the state needs to have limits. One of those limits is this kind of due process. Usually, the government doesn't bring BS cases, but you know what, sometimes it does. Sometimes they bring cases that are not well-founded, and the allegations aren't proven, and we just have to move the pack on and recognize that in this one case, united healthcare didn't do what they were accused of. Frustrating as it can be for people who feel in their heart that a big company has done something wrong, that same due process protects us, in our hour of need, when the government comes after us for reasons dubious. United can hire more lawyers than the average citizen, but everybody deserves to process between them and an angry or vengeful state.

In this case, a federal Special Master recommended to a judge that the DOJ had not made its case. The allegation was that United had used “up-coding”—creating fictitious diagnoses to increase the rate it was paid for Medicare advantage claims come to the tune of over $2 billion in additional money for diagnoses the patients didn't have. However, this case only included behavior alleged between 2009 and 2016. That was a long time ago:

The DOJ alleges Medicare paid UnitedHealth Group more than $7.2 billion from 2009 through 2016 based on the company’s efforts to boost revenue by reviewing patient records to find additional diagnoses and adding medical billing codes to their files. According to the DOJ, Medicare would have paid the company $2.1 billion less if it had deleted unsupported billing codes.

Suzanne Sengal is the Special Master appointed to the case. She is not the judge in this matter, but she recommended the judge accept United's motion for dismissal:

“A mere possibility of an overpayment is not enough for the government to carry its burden,” Sagal stated.

Before we do an unvarnished victory lap for the team at UnitedHealth Group, it's important to point out that they're facing ongoing scrutiny for just this kind of behavior in places that are not California and not in the time period between 2009 and 2016. In fact, there are additional investigations happening right now for other conduct on their part in other places that may meet the level of criminal or civil liability.

If you're a massive company, such as the biggest healthcare company on earth, you're going to get sued a lot. That's just what's happening. Ideally, you don't do anything wrong, and so none of those lawsuits go anywhere. Less ideally, you've done something that's a problem, and you have to spend a lot of shareholders’ money on lawyers to defend yourselves from the Department of Justice attempting to take your money away, and maybe, just maybe, put you in jail.

We don't actually have to wonder if the public thinks United healthcare is guilty. The public doesn't even know the difference between UnitedHealth Group and United Healthcare— but when a senior executive is murdered, they're cheering for the murder all day long. This is disgusting, horrifying, and what's happening. Right now.

So my advice to UnitedHealth Group—celebrate this one. But, right after that, cooperate with the government to settle any pending cases, and start treating your plan members and many, many patients as well as 10% of all physicians in your employ a little bit better. Start treating healthcare as if it was your baby, because, practically, it kind of is. You need to treat healthcare like it's something that we all need to have intact— not just now, but in the future. It needs to be more than just profitable in this quarter. It needs to be safe, effective, and even profitable long into the future. That may mean, accepting a little bit less profits now, or spending less of those profits on legal bills, and perhaps spending a little bit more on making sure the care we provide is valuable to the people who need it.

United healthcare employs so many people, it boggles the mind. It helps take care of so many patients, it beggars belief. And it would be a better world, for everybody, if United Healthcare and UnitedHealth Group, the parent organization, did a great job of covering care, did a great job of providing care, and if everybody was happy with them, because healthcare was great under their leadership.

When the Department of Justice is investigating relentlessly, and citizens are cheering for the murder of your employees, which again, I decry, there's something wrong.

For today, congratulations on beating an unfounded case! l Let's everyone join United celebrating the fact that they were not convicted or found guilty of fraud, in this one case. We can then encourage them to commit no fraud! We can clap for joy when they take great care of their patient, employees, plan members, and customers, ever onward. Let's celebrate the people at UnitedHealth Group as they try to make things right.

Congratulations, and you've got work to do. We all do, healthcare is complicated, and we need to work together.
